analysis.one_liner: Funds rental aid and permanently affordable housing by trimming tax breaks for higher-income homeowners and inherited wealth.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a single committee vote or cosponsor when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, one month after it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cap the mortgage interest and property tax deductions for households earning over $75,000, repeal the rule that lets inherited property escape capital gains tax, and deposit the resulting revenue into a new federal Housing Trust Fund. The fund would pay guaranteed grants to states, large cities and counties, and Indian tribes for two programs: rental and home-purchase assistance that caps low-income families' housing costs, and construction or rehabilitation of housing that must stay affordable for its entire useful life. It was referred to two House committees, then to subcommittees, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income families who pay more than 30 percent of income for housing would get help covering rent or mortgage payments, with aid paid directly to landlords or mortgage servicers. Communities would gain new affordable units built or rehabbed with binding lifetime affordability restrictions, plus lead-paint abatement and emergency repairs. States, entitlement communities, and tribes get funding weighted toward areas where families pay over half their income for housing, with reserved help for minority families moving out of high-poverty areas. Local boards would have to include a formerly homeless person and low-income housing advocates.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the mortgage interest and property tax deductions for taxpayers with adjusted gross income over $75,000, phasing the deduction down toward a 50 percent floor by 2000, and credits the resulting revenue to a new Housing Trust Fund.

Creates an entitlement: every qualifying state, large city or county, and Indian tribe is entitled to an annual grant, allocated by formula based on the share of families paying more than 50 percent of income for housing and on local shortages of affordable units.

Requires a housing costs assistance program that pays the gap between fair market rent and the lesser of 30 percent of a family's adjusted income or 5 percent of gross income, with payments made to the landlord or mortgage servicer and counseling for assisted families.

Requires a housing supply assistance program funding acquisition, construction, and rehabilitation of affordable housing that must remain affordable for the entire useful life of the property, with lead-paint abatement and emergency repairs also eligible.

Sets priorities for extremely low-income families, requires resident and citizen participation in local decisions, requires a formerly homeless person and low-income housing advocates on each local administering board, and reserves up to 20 percent of rental aid for minority families moving to areas without concentrated poverty.
Repeals the stepped-up basis rule so inherited property is taxed on gains accrued during the decedent's lifetime, phased in from 10 percent in 1996 to 25 percent in 1999.

analysis.who_pays: Households with adjusted gross income over $75,000 would see their mortgage interest and property tax deductions shrink. People inheriting appreciated property would owe capital gains tax on gains that previously went untaxed at death. The $75,000 threshold is in 1994 dollars and would also reach upper-middle-income homeowners, especially in high-cost areas.

drawbacks.text: The $75,000 income threshold is a blunt cutoff: a homeowner family at or slightly above that income, particularly in an expensive housing market, would lose part of its mortgage interest and property tax deductions even though the housing it owns is not luxury housing.

Repealing stepped-up basis would create real compliance burdens and could force heirs of small businesses or farms to sell assets to pay capital gains tax on gains their parents never realized, which is why the carryover-basis proposal has repeatedly failed in Congress.

The rental-assistance design pays landlords directly and guarantees them tenants with covered rent, which can bid up rents in tight markets and channel public money to private owners; the bill caps local administrative costs at 6 percent but leaves landlord profits largely unaddressed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a large, permanent funding stream for rental aid and affordable housing, paid for by narrowing two tax preferences that mostly benefit higher-income households. The aid side is well targeted: formula grants go where housing burdens are worst, units built with the money must stay affordable permanently, and low-income residents get a formal seat in local decisions. The cost side has genuine design problems: the $75,000 threshold would claw back deductions from upper-middle-income homeowners rather than only the wealthy, and taxing inherited gains creates valuation and liquidity problems for heirs of illiquid assets. On balance a defensible proposal, though the tax side could have been better targeted.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in early October 1994 with no cosponsors, referred to two committees and then to subcommittees, and the 103rd Congress ended before either committee took any action on it.

narrative.text: Representative Major Owens introduced the bill on October 7, 1994, less than a month before the midterm election.
It was referred the same day to both the Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, the split reflecting its two halves: a housing program and a tax change.
No member of the House cosponsored the bill.
On November 8, 1994, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Housing and Community Development and the Subcommittee on Economic Growth and Credit Formation, where the record ends.
Neither committee ever held a markup or reported the bill, and it never received a floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Higher-income households kept the mortgage interest and property tax deductions above $75,000 of income, and heirs kept the untaxed step-up in basis on inherited property; no new affordable-housing funding was created.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded and no member joined as a cosponsor, so the partisan split never took shape; the bill was a lone Democratic sponsorship with no Republican or Democratic co-supporters on the record.

industries.note: The bill phases down their mortgage interest and property tax deductions to help fund housing aid. The cost falls partly on upper-middle-income owners in high-cost areas, not only the wealthy.

industries.industry: Heirs and holders of inherited wealth
industries.note: Repealing stepped-up basis means gains accrued during a decedent's lifetime would be taxed when heirs sell, phased in from 10 to 25 percent between 1996 and 1999. This closes a major preference for inherited assets.

Rental and purchase assistance is paid directly to owners and servicers on behalf of assisted families, guaranteeing them payment streams. The aid helps tenants afford housing but also subsidizes private owners and can support rents.

industries.industry: Affordable housing developers, including nonprofits and for-profit providers
industries.note: The supply program funds acquisition, construction, and rehabilitation, open to nonprofits, cooperatives, public agencies, and for-profit providers, with units locked into affordability for life. Their revenue grows in step with the public purpose.
